The Mystery Crystal Revealed!

Last time, we ended on a bit of a cliffhanger. We did a hands-on activity where you all tried to cut a shiny, mystery crystal. We had some great guesses today—graphite was a huge favorite, along with metal, metalloid, and glass.

But it isn’t graphite. The mystery crystal is Silicon.

Silicon wafers are perhaps the most amazing mass-produced material on Earth. Let’s talk about why this material is so special:

  • Atomically Flat: These wafers are polished to an average roughness of just a fraction of a nanometer (about 0.2 nanometers). To put that in perspective, we are talking about the size scale of individual atoms. The surface is so flat that it looks like a flawless mirror.

  • Incredibly Pure: We can control the chemical composition of these crystals to an astonishing degree. We can make silicon so pure that there is only one contaminant atom for every 10 billion silicon atoms. In real-life speak, 10^{10} is 10 billion. The entire human population on Earth is about 8 billion. Imagine if only one single person on the entire planet was different from the rest—that is the level of purity we are talking about!

Why does this matter? Because this extremely flat, highly pure silicon is the foundational canvas for modern electronics. It allows us to manufacture computer chips over a large area. On a modern, state-of-the-art computer chip (about the size of your fingernail), we can pack in roughly 10 billion transistors. Transistors are tiny electronic switches that shuttle, store, and calculate digital information. Fitting 10^{10} of them onto a tiny chip is only possible because we have such an incredible material to build on.

From Sand to Super-Chips

You might have heard that silicon is made from sand, and that is essentially true! Sand is mostly silicon oxide. The trick is separating the oxygen from the silicon and then purifying it to that ridiculous "one-in-10-billion" standard.

To do this, manufacturers use a fancy synthesis technique called the Czochralski process.

Through this process, we pull a massive, cylindrical chunk of silicon called an ingot. Once we have this giant ingot, we slice it up into thin wafers, kind of like slicing a cucumber. After slicing, the wafers undergo sophisticated mechanical and chemical polishing to achieve that atomically flat surface we just talked about.

Crystal Lattices and the Art of Cleaving

Let’s go back to our cutting activity. I noticed a lot of squeaks, scratches, and sadness as crystals shattered instead of breaking cleanly. Why was it so hard to cut?

It all comes down to what a crystal actually is. When we say "crystal," we mean that the atoms are arranged in a highly organized, repeating, orderly pattern—what we call a lattice. This is the opposite of an amorphous material, like glass, where the atoms are just jumbled up in a messy blob.

If you look closely at a silicon wafer, you will notice it is not a flawless circle; it has a distinct flat edge on one side. That flat edge is a physical guide to the invisible atomic lattice inside.

Imagine zooming in on the wafer until you can see the atoms, just like in the sketch above. They are arranged in a neat, square-like grid. If you make a tiny scratch parallel or perpendicular to that flat edge, you are aligning your cut straight down the "aisles" of the atomic grid. When you apply pressure, the crystal easily cracks along that straight line because you are just breaking the bonds between the rows of atoms. It is much easier and cleaner to cut this way!

However, if you try to cut at a random angle, your cut is trying to plow diagonally through the atoms themselves. You cannot cut through solid atoms! Instead, the break jumps jaggedly from one row to the next, resulting in a shattered, unpredictable edge. This cleaving behavior is actually a wonderful, indirect piece of evidence that atoms exist and are arranged in a discrete, orderly lattice.

The Shrinking Game: 1D Length Scales

To really understand nanoscience, we need to build an intuition for how small things actually are. We are going to play a game called the Shrinking Game, where we step down in size by factors of 10.

First, let’s introduce a symbol you will see a lot in this class: \sim. This squiggle means "on the order of" or "very roughly."

Let’s start with a human. I am a bit on the shorter side, and Shaquille O’Neal is a giant at over 2 meters tall, but order-of-magnitude wise, we can round humans to being \sim 1 meter tall.

Now, let’s shrink by a factor of 10. This is also called changing by one order of magnitude. It just means we are dividing our length by 10 (or taking away one digit).

  • Human: \sim 1 meter.

  • Baseball: Shrink a human by a factor of 10, and you get something \sim 10^{-1} meters, which is 10 centimeters. The diameter of a baseball fits this nicely.

  • Dice: Shrink by another factor of 10. Now we are at \sim 10^{-2} meters, or 1 centimeter. A standard board game die is right on the money.

  • Sesame Seed: Shrink by another factor of 10. We hit \sim 10^{-3} meters, which is 1 millimeter.

  • Human Hair / Thread: Shrink by one more factor of 10. We are at \sim 10^{-4} meters. This is a tenth of a millimeter (0.1 mm), or 100 micrometers (\mum). A fine sewing thread or a strand of human hair lives at this scale.

Unit Conversion the Easy Way

You might be wondering how we confidently jump between meters, centimeters, and millimeters. Let’s walk through a foolproof way to convert units using our baseball example.

We know the baseball is 10^{-1} meters. We want to find out what that is in centimeters.

First, write down the conversion fact you know. We know that the prefix "centi" means 10^{-2}. Therefore: \begin{equation*} 1 \text{ cm} = 10^{-2} \text{ m} \end{equation*}

To convert our baseball’s size, we take our starting value (10^{-1} m) and multiply it by a fraction that equals 1. We put the unit we want to kill off (meters) on the bottom, and the unit we want to keep (centimeters) on the top:

\begin{align*} 10^{-1} \text{ m} &= 10^{-1} \text{ m} \times \left( \frac{1 \text{ cm}}{10^{-2} \text{ m}} \right) \end{align*}

Because 1 \text{ cm} and 10^{-2} \text{ m} are the exact same length, that fraction is just a fancy way of writing the number 1. Multiplying by 1 doesn’t change the actual physical size of the object.

Notice that we have meters on the top and meters on the bottom, so they cancel out, leaving us with just centimeters:

\begin{align*} &= \frac{10^{-1}}{10^{-2}} \text{ cm} \end{align*}

Now we just use basic exponent math. When you divide numbers with exponents, you subtract the bottom exponent from the top exponent:

\begin{align*} &= 10^{-1 - (-2)} \text{ cm} \\ &= 10^{-1 + 2} \text{ cm} \\ &= 10^1 \text{ cm} \\ &= 10 \text{ cm} \end{align*}

And there we have it! A baseball is 10 centimeters across. If you ever panic on a quiz about unit conversions, just fall back on this method. Write down what you know, arrange the fraction to kill off the unit you don’t want, and let the exponent math do the heavy lifting for you.

Continuing the Shrinking Game: Into the Nanoscale

Now that we have our unit conversion skills warmed up, let’s continue our shrinking game. In class, we did a fun activity where we kept shrinking our 1D length scale by 10 times (one order of magnitude) at every single step, diving deep into the microscopic and nanoscopic worlds.

Here are the scales we looked at:

  • \sim 10 \ \mum (10^{-5} m)

  • \sim 1 \ \mum (10^{-6} m)

  • \sim 100 nm (10^{-7} m)

  • \sim 10 nm (10^{-8} m)

  • \sim 1 nm (10^{-9} m)

  • \sim 0.1 nm = 1 angstrom (10^{-10} m)

I gave you a list of tiny objects and asked you to take turns drawing and labeling them on the board at the correct scale. The objects were:

  • atom

  • human red blood cell

  • COVID virus

  • e-coli bacterium

  • lipid bilayer (cell membrane)

  • simple sugar molecule (e.g., glucose)

How did you do? Here are the solutions!

  • \sim 10 \ \mum (10^{-5} m): [diameter of] human red blood cell

  • \sim 1 \ \mum (10^{-6} m): [length of] e-coli bacterium

  • \sim 100 nm (10^{-7} m): [diameter of] COVID virus. Coach’s tip: Remember that most viruses are smaller than bacteria!

  • \sim 10 nm (10^{-8} m): [thickness of] lipid bilayer (cell membrane)

  • \sim 1 nm (10^{-9} m): [width of] simple sugar molecule (e.g., glucose)

  • \sim 0.1 nm = 1 angstrom (10^{-10} m): [diameter of] atom

Before we wrap up this section, let’s clear up a vocabulary distinction that often trips students up: the difference between a factor of a number and orders of magnitude. Let’s use the human red blood cell and the COVID virus to see how this works.

The red blood cell is \sim 10^{-5} meters across. The COVID virus is \sim 10^{-7} meters across.

If we want to know how many orders of magnitude different they are, we just find the difference between their exponents. We take the red blood cell’s exponent and subtract the virus’s exponent: \begin{align*} \text{Difference} &= -5 - (-7) \\ &= -5 + 7 \\ &= 2 \end{align*} Because the difference is 2, they are separated by 2 orders of magnitude. You can think of "orders of magnitude" as simply counting the steps on our shrinking ladder, or counting the number of tens we are multiplying together.

But what if I ask for the factor? A "factor" is the actual, everyday number you multiply or divide by to get from one size to the other. Since they are 2 orders of magnitude apart, we use that 2 as our exponent for 10: \begin{align*} \text{Factor} &= 10^2 \\ &= 10 \times 10 \\ &= 100 \end{align*} So, the red blood cell is larger by a factor of 100.

To put it in a real-world picture: "Orders of magnitude" tells us we took two jumps down our scale of tens. The "factor of 100" tells us that if you lined up COVID viruses end-to-end, it would take 100 of them to stretch across a single red blood cell!
